question: Can I replace a window with a same-size double-pane window on the part of the house over the property line?
answer:
I can't give you a yes or no from the code alone. Whether this needs a design review permit or a variance is something city planning staff would have to decide. Here is what the code and city policy say.

**Code says:** A house that was built legally but doesn't meet today's rules is a "nonconforming structure." Repairs are covered:
> 1. Maintenance and repair. Routine maintenance and repairs may be performed on a nonconforming structure.

Changes are limited:
> An existing nonconforming structure may be altered or enlarged without variance as long as the alteration or enlargement does not relate to or involve the nonconformity. If an alteration or enlargement does relate to or involve a nonconformity of a non-conforming structure, a variance is required under division 17.70.

The code also defines "replacement" narrowly:
> Replacement means rebuilding all or a portion of an improvement to be exactly the same as what was replaced.

— Piedmont City Code §17.50.020

A window that is the same size but double-pane isn't "exactly the same" if the old one is single-pane. So it's unclear whether it counts as routine repair or as an alteration that involves the over-the-line part of the house.

If the part over the line sits on **city property or a city easement**, other rules apply:
> No building permit will be issued for construction by a person other than the city or a public utility on or over city property or a city easement unless an encroachment permit has first been obtained from the Director of Public Works.

— Piedmont City Code §17.06.050

**City policy says:** Some window replacements don't need a design review permit at all. That includes ordinary repairs:
> 4. Normal repairs, replacement and maintenance of existing construction, so long as there is no change in the materials, design and size of the feature being repaired or replaced.

— Piedmont Design Guidelines, page 2-7

It also includes certain clad-wood windows:
> 32. The replacement of an existing wood window or door with a new window or door made of wood with aluminum or fiberglass exterior cladding, provided that there is no change in the following:
> a. The size or location of the window or door.
> b. The operation of the window or door.
> c. The recess of the window or door from the exterior wall surface.
> d. The divided lite pattern (if any), provided that any new divided lites are either true divided lites or 3-dimensional simulated divided lites.

— Piedmont Design Guidelines, page 2-11

The city's window policy also says:
> 6. Support the use of energy efficient windows.

— Window Replacement Policy, page 1

**Needs staff:**
1. Is a same-size, double-pane replacement on the over-the-line part "routine maintenance and repair," or an alteration that "relates to or involves the nonconformity" and needs a variance?
2. Does it qualify for one of the design review exceptions above, or does it need an Expedited Design Review Permit?

**To narrow this down, I need to know:**
- **Your address and zone.** You haven't entered your property details yet, so I don't know your zoning.
- **Where the over-the-line part sits:** on a neighbor's lot, or on city property or a city easement.
- **The current window and the new one:** frame material (wood, clad wood, vinyl) and whether the operation and divided-lite pattern stay the same.

question: How do I show the side setback where the house crosses the property line?
answer:
The plan guidelines and code cover the basics. Neither says how to dimension a wall that sits on or past the lot line, so that part needs a staff answer.

**City policy says:** Your site plans need to show setback dimensions from each structure to the lot lines. For the existing site plan:
> Provide setback dimensions from all existing structures to lot lines (Setback means the required distance that a building, structure or other designated item must be located from a lot line. Setbacks are measured from the lot line to the footprint of the structure or building. See Zoning Ordinance Sec. 17.90.020.)

— Piedmont Design Guidelines, page 2-13 (PDF page 24)

The same page asks for the proposed site plan to:
> outline the locations of structures on adjacent properties (up to 25 feet from the property line) and label their uses.

For new construction, it also asks for a site survey:
> a. Please dimension and show coordinates for all lot lines.

**Code says:** The definition measures from the lot line to the footprint:
> Setbacks are measured from the lot line to the footprint of the structure or building.

— Piedmont City Code §17.90.020

"Footprint" is measured from the outside of the exterior walls. Some eaves and overhangs are left out:
> Eave and/or roof overhang that projects up to three feet from the exterior wall surface or supporting column or post;

— Piedmont City Code §17.90.020

This means you need to know which part of the house crosses the line. A wall counts toward the footprint. An eave that sticks out 3 feet or less doesn't.

**Needs staff:** The knowledge base doesn't say how to label a setback when the footprint crosses the lot line. For example, it doesn't say whether to write a negative number (like "−0'-8\" (encroaches)"), write "0 ft" and note the encroachment, or require a survey. Planning staff will need to answer that. It may also matter how the code treats an existing structure that doesn't meet setback rules (§17.50.020, Nonconforming structure), but I haven't pulled up that section's full text, so I can't say how it applies.

In the meantime, a clear way to draw it is to show the surveyed lot line and outline the part of the house that crosses it. Then note how far it extends past the line, and label whether that part is a wall or an eave. This is a suggestion only, not a city rule.

question: What counts as floor area?
answer:
**Code says:** Piedmont defines floor area in the Measurements section:

> Floor area of a building means the sum of the gross horizontal area of the floors of the building, measured from the exterior faces of exterior walls or from the center line of party walls separating two buildings, and includes, but is not limited to:

— Piedmont City Code §17.90.020

The code then lists what is included:

> 1. living space on all levels, including within a basement or attic;
> 2. elevator shafts and stairwells at each floor;
> 3. bay window or window seat that projects beyond the exterior wall in which a person can reasonably stand or sit, even if the window or seat does not have a minimum ceiling height of seven feet, six inches;
> 4. seventy square feet or more of contiguous non-habitable attic area that has permanent access, a minimum ceiling height of five feet, and an average ceiling height of at least seven feet six inches. Permanent access includes built-in stairs (even if they do not meet all of the building code requirements), but does not include built-in or pull-down ladders;
> 5. seventy square feet or more of contiguous non-habitable basement area that has a minimum ceiling height of seven feet and at least 42 inches of the basement level, measured from the basement ceiling, is above grade at the exterior wall;
> 6. enclosed porch or lanai, heated or not;
> 7. high-volume space that exceeds an average height of 15 feet, measured from finished floor to the outer roof, is counted as two stories; and
> 8. area within a building used for commercial purposes.

— Piedmont City Code §17.90.020

It also says what is generally left out, with some limits:

> Unless listed above, living space not considered habitable under the Building Code because of window size, ventilation, access, ceiling height, heating, or electrical service (e.g. unconditioned storage area) is not counted in the floor area, but if the space is actually used for living, sleeping, eating, bathing, washing, or cooking, the space will be included, subject to the interpretation of the Director. Mechanical rooms containing gas-burning furnaces or gas-burning hot water heaters are not considered a living space.

— Piedmont City Code §17.90.020

**In short:**
- Measure from the outside faces of the exterior walls.
- Count all living space, including basements and attics.
- Count stairwells and elevator shafts on every floor.
- Count enclosed porches.
- Count some unfinished attic and basement areas once they reach 70 sq ft and meet the height rules above.
- Rooms over 15 feet tall on average count twice.
- Unconditioned storage generally doesn't count, unless it's actually used as living space.

**City policy says:** Floor area is used to work out your floor area ratio (FAR):

> c. Existing and proposed floor area ratio (FAR) equals the number of square feet of floor area divided by the number of square feet in the lot. For a complete definition of floor area, please see Zoning Ordinance Sec. 17.90.020.

— Piedmont Design Guidelines, page 2-15 (PDF page 26)

question: Will the city approve my variance?
answer:

>     property (including but not limited to size, shape, topography, location and surroundings),
>     so that strictly applying the terms of this chapter would keep the property from being used in
>     the same manner as other conforming properties in the zone;
>     2. The project is compatible with the immediately surrounding neighborhood and the public

>     3. Accomplishing the improvement without a variance would cause unreasonable hardship
>     in planning, design, or construction. In this subsection 3, unreasonable hardship refers to
>     the unusual physical characteristics of the property and existing improvements, and not to
>     conditions personal to the applicant. (See also Reasonable accommodation, at division

question: Isn't the side setback for ADUs 4 feet?
answer:
Yes, the code sets 4 feet for a newly built ADU. It doesn't apply in every case, though. A conversion or same-size rebuild needs no setback at all, and street-facing yards follow different rules.

**Code says:** The ADU rules in §17.38.060 set two different side and rear setbacks:

> b. Side and Rear Setbacks. No setback is required to construct an accessory dwelling unit within an existing structure that is converted to an accessory dwelling unit or a new structure constructed in the same location and the same dimension as an existing structure. If an accessory dwelling unit is not converted from an existing structure, the minimum setback is four feet from the side and rear lot line.

— Piedmont City Code §17.38.060.B.6.b

- **New ADU** (not a conversion): at least 4 feet from the side and rear lot lines.
- **Converting an existing structure, or rebuilding in the same location and same dimensions**: no setback required.

**Code says:** The Zone A rules say the same thing and compare it to the normal 5-foot setback:

> Minimum 5 feet for a primary or accessory structure, unless the yard is street facing, in which case the minimum is 20 feet, except that a setback of only 4 feet is required for a new structure to be used as an accessory dwelling unit, and no setback is required for conversions of an existing structure to an accessory dwelling unit or portion thereof in the same location and same dimensions.

— Piedmont City Code §17.20.040

**Code says:** A street-facing yard is handled separately. ADUs up to 800 sq ft may go in the street yard setback, but larger ones only in limited cases:

> Accessory dwelling units of more than 800 square feet can be constructed in the street yard setback only if it is determined by the Director that there is no alternative configuration on the property that would allow for the construction of the accessory dwelling unit outside the four feet side and rear setbacks in compliance with all other standards in this section, including height.

— Piedmont City Code §17.38.060.B.6.c

**Code says:** For a junior ADU (JADU) that adds up to 150 sq ft to an accessory structure for an entrance or exit, the code requires:
